History & Physical (H&P – Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
38-year-old woman with 3-day history of profuse watery/loose diarrhoea, repeated vomiting, subjective fever, and periumbilical pain after contact with symptomatic brother, clinically felt to be infectious gastroenteritis with plans for stool culture and hydration assessment.

History:
• Presenting complaint – Severe diarrhoea “very loose, initially watery,” onset 3 days ago.  
• Frequency – “Lost count,” ≥4 bowel motions today.  
• Vomiting – Recurrent; unable to retain food, water, or ORS; last episode ~2 h before call (after breakfast).  
• Fever – Subjective feeling “literally boiling;” no thermometer reading.  
• Abdominal pain – Periumbilical tenderness; colicky, coincides with urge to defecate.  
• Urinary status – Passing urine; last void 1 h ago; colour unknown; no dysuria or hematuria.  
• Blood in stool/urine – Denied.  
• Rash – Denied.  
• Prior bowel pattern – Daily, formed stool; no prior similar episodes or chronic GI symptoms.  
• Exposure – Brother with identical illness; reports school outbreak. No recent travel.  
• System review / pertinent negatives  
  – Constitutional: No documented weight loss.  
  – Respiratory: No cough, SOB.  
  – Cardiovascular: No chest pain, palpitations.  
  – GI: As above; no hematemesis, no jaundice.  
  – GU: Normal frequency/flow.  
  – Dermatologic: No rash.  
  – Neurologic: No headache, photophobia.  

Past Medical History:
• Generally healthy; no chronic illnesses reported.  
• Gynaecologic: Normal menses; dysmenorrhoea treated with ibuprofen.  
• Surgical history: None.  
• Obstetric: Not discussed.  
• Complications: None reported.

Medications:
• Vitamin D supplement – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Oral Rehydration Solution (salt-sugar mix) – approx. three times daily for the last 2 days.  
• Ibuprofen – dose/route/frequency not documented; taken occasionally for menstrual cramps.

Allergies:
• Not discussed – missing.

Social History:
• Occupation – Graphic designer; working from home today due to illness.  
• Living situation – Resides with brother and mother.  
• Tobacco – Non-smoker.  
• Alcohol – Occasional; “a pint from time to time.”  
• Recreational drugs – Denied.  
• Sexual activity – Not currently sexually active; no contraception.  
• Travel – No recent travel abroad.  

Family History:
• Brother acutely ill with similar diarrhoea & vomiting; possible communal school outbreak.  
• No other family history obtained.

Physical Examination:
(Tele-consultation – limited)  
• General: Appears unwell by history.  
• Vital signs: Not measured.  
• Abdomen: Reported marked tenderness around umbilicus.  
• Skin: No rash reported.  
• Hydration: Able to void urine an hour prior; otherwise not formally assessed.

Investigations:
• None completed at time of call.  
• Planned: Stool sample for culture/analysis; in-clinic assessment of hydration status.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1 – Acute diarrhoea & vomiting – probable infectious gastroenteritis (viral most likely; bacterial not excluded).  
  • Arrange urgent clinic appointment for physical review and stool specimen collection.  
  • Continue Oral Rehydration Solution; advise tiny frequent sips.  
  • Simple diet: toast, plain biscuits; avoid fruit, vegetables, dairy until improved.  
  • Educate on expected course; most viral cases self-limiting.  

Issue 2 – Risk of dehydration.  
  • Clinic visit to check hydration (pulse, BP, mucous membranes, capillary refill).  
  • Red-flag advice: if unable to tolerate fluids, reduced urine output, worsening abdominal pain, altered consciousness, seek emergency care (A&E).  

Issue 3 – Rule-out bacterial enteritis.  
  • Send stool culture; consider targeted antibiotics if pathogen identified and clinically indicated.  

General follow-up:  
• Patient to book same-day urgent clinic slot via support line.  
• 24-hour helpline / call-back if deterioration.  

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
1. Acute viral gastroenteritis (likely norovirus) – High likelihood: abrupt onset, household clustering, watery diarrhoea/vomiting, no blood.  
2. Acute bacterial gastroenteritis (Campylobacter/Salmonella/E. coli) – Moderate likelihood: persistent symptoms >72 h, subjective fever, abdominal pain; stool culture planned.  
3. Food-borne toxin–mediated illness – Low–moderate: vomiting prominent but usually resolves <24 h; persistence and person-to-person spread make this less probable.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: documented allergies, objective vitals (temp, HR, BP), complete medication reconciliation (doses), urine colour, formal fluid balance.  
● No explicit conflicts between transcript and DDx noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear overall; occasional brief inaudible pauses, but clinical content intact.
